Mercia
MUR-shuh
n. (the midland Anglo-Saxon kingdom, last of the English realms to be converted, and supreme in England in the eighth century)
Latinised from Old English Mierce, the borderers or march people, from mearc, a boundary.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Mercia was the kingdom of the English midlands, named from the border people, and it was the last of the great English realms to receive the gospel. Penda, who ruled it from about 626 to 655, was the most formidable heathen king in English history: he killed Edwin and Oswald of Northumbria and Sigebert and Anna of East Anglia in battle, and he died fighting Oswiu at the Winwaed. He did not persecute Christians, and Bede notes that he allowed preachers in his kingdom and despised only converts who did not keep the faith they professed. His son Peada was baptised before his death, his sons Wulfhere and Ethelred were Christian, Chad was given Lichfield as his see, and under Offa in the later eighth century Mercia dominated England and briefly had an archbishopric of its own at Lichfield. The dictionary records Mercia because Penda is the clearest English case of a ruler who is no friend of the church and whom God nevertheless uses. Scripture insists on this repeatedly: the king's heart is in the LORD'S hand, Nebuchadnezzar is called his servant, Assyria is the rod of his anger, and the powers that be are ordained of God.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a king as a chief ruler; a heart as the seat of the will and affections; a rod as an instrument of correction; a power as one invested with authority; and to ordain as to appoint and establish.

expand to see more

KING, n. The chief or sovereign of a nation; a man invested with supreme authority over a nation, tribe or country.

HEART, n. The seat of the affections and passions; the will; the seat of understanding and of purpose.

ROD, n. The instrument of punishment or correction; hence, punishment or chastisement; also, a staff of authority.

POWER, n. Command; the right of governing; one who is invested with authority; a ruling magistrate or state.

ORDAIN, v.t. To appoint; to decree; to establish; to institute; to set in order.

Key Scripture

Pro 21:1 — "The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will."

Jer 27:6 — "And now have I given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant; and the beasts of the field have I given him also to serve him."

Isa 10:5 — "O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger, and the staff in their hand is mine indignation."

Rom 13:1 — "Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God."

Modern Corruption

The midland Anglo-Saxon kingdom of the border people, held by the heathen Penda until 655 and supreme in England under Offa.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God governs rulers who do not acknowledge him. Solomon states the mechanism without qualification: “The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will” (Pro 21:1). Jeremiah is made to call a pagan conqueror by a startling title, “Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant” (Jer 27:6).

The live temptation is to read political history as though the church's fortunes depended on having friendly kings. Penda was not friendly and the gospel entered his kingdom anyway; Offa was baptised and used the church as an instrument of his power. Isaiah addresses an empire that had no idea whose purposes it served, “O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger” (Isa 10:5). Paul draws the practical conclusion for Christians under any government whatever, in a letter written while Nero reigned: “For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew leb (H3820), the heart or will; Hebrew ebed (H5650), a servant; Hebrew shebet (H7626), a rod; Greek exousia (G1849), authority.

expand to see more

Hebrew leb (H3820) — the heart, the will; “The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD”, Proverbs 21:1.

Hebrew natah (H5186) — to stretch out, to turn; “he turneth it whithersoever he will”, Proverbs 21:1.

Hebrew ebed (H5650) — a servant, a bondman; “Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant”, Jeremiah 27:6.

Hebrew shebet (H7626) — a rod, a sceptre; “the rod of mine anger”, Isaiah 10:5.

Greek exousia (G1849) — authority, a ruling power; “there is no power but of God”, Romans 13:1.

Usage

"“The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD” (Pro 21:1) — including Penda's."

"“Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant” (Jer 27:6) — a heathen so titled."

"“the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1) — written under Nero."
